name: Western trade-hub relay
what: The richest crossroads of the western Old World and then the Atlantic, handed on from city to city for 4,500 years.
why: Shows that the centre of trade keeps moving, and that wars, silt and new sea routes move it.

legs.why: Middleman between Mesopotamia, Magan (Oman copper) and Meluhha (the Indus); Ur's merchants bought copper here.

sources.cite: Harriet Crawford, Dilmun and its Gulf Neighbours (Cambridge UP, 1998)

legs.lost: Indus trade collapsed and Gulf trade shrank after about 1750 BCE.

legs.why: Port of the Late Bronze Age system linking Egypt, the Hittites, Cyprus copper and the Aegean; its archives list merchants from all of them.

sources.cite: Marc Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (3rd ed., 2016)

legs.lost: Destroyed around 1185 BCE in the Late Bronze Age collapse.

legs.why: Phoenician hub for purple dye, cedar and silver, founding colonies from Cyprus to Gades.

sources.cite: Maria Eugenia Aubet, The Phoenicians and the West (2nd ed., Cambridge UP, 2001)

legs.lost: Taken by Alexander after a seven-month siege in 332 BCE.

legs.why: Tyre's colony became the hub of the western Mediterranean, controlling Spanish silver and Sardinian grain.

sources.cite: Richard Miles, Carthage Must Be Destroyed (2010)
David Abulafia, The Great Sea: A Human History of the Mediterranean (2011)

legs.lost: Razed by Rome in 146 BCE at the end of the Third Punic War.

legs.why: Egypt's grain and the Red Sea route to India met the Mediterranean here; the Periplus describes the India trade it fed.

sources.cite: W. V. Harris and Giovanni Ruffini (eds), Ancient Alexandria between Egypt and Greece (2004)
Lionel Casson, The Periplus Maris Erythraei (Princeton UP, 1989)

legs.lost: Lost the lead as the western empire broke up and Constantinople grew.

legs.why: Capital on the Bosporus between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean and between Europe and Asia.

sources.cite: Angeliki Laiou and Cecile Morrisson, The Byzantine Economy (Cambridge UP, 2007)

legs.lost: Sacked by the Fourth Crusade in 1204, and its trade passed to Venice.

legs.why: Abbasid capital where Gulf shipping and Silk Road caravans met; the hub of the Islamic world economy.

sources.cite: Hugh Kennedy, When Baghdad Ruled the Muslim World (2005)

legs.lost: Abbasid decline moved the trade toward Fatimid Cairo and the Red Sea.

legs.why: Held the spice trade from Alexandria and the Levant into Europe through its state-run galley convoys.

sources.cite: Frederic Lane, Venice: A Maritime Republic (Johns Hopkins UP, 1973)
Janet Abu-Lughod, Before European Hegemony: The World System A.D. 1250-1350 (Oxford UP, 1989)

legs.lost: Da Gama's sea route to India (1498) moved the pepper trade to the Atlantic.

legs.why: Northern counterpart to Venice, where Italian galleys met the Hansa; an early home of the bourse.

sources.cite: James Murray, Bruges, Cradle of Capitalism, 1280-1390 (Cambridge UP, 2005)

legs.lost: The Zwin channel silted up and trade moved to Antwerp.

legs.why: Portuguese spices, south German silver and English cloth met here; the centre of the world economy in the early 1500s.

sources.cite: Herman Van der Wee, The Growth of the Antwerp Market and the European Economy (1963)
Fernand Braudel, Civilization and Capitalism, 15th-18th Century, vol. 3: The Perspective of the World (1979)

legs.lost: Spanish sack (1576), siege (1585) and the Dutch closing of the Scheldt.

legs.why: The VOC (1602), the Bank of Amsterdam (1609) and the Baltic grain trade made it the world's warehouse and money market.

sources.cite: Jonathan Israel, Dutch Primacy in World Trade, 1585-1740 (Oxford UP, 1989)
Fernand Braudel, Civilization and Capitalism, 15th-18th Century, vol. 3: The Perspective of the World (1979)

legs.lost: Lost out to London over the 1700s and fell to French invasion in 1795.

legs.why: Empire, the industrial revolution and sterling made the City the world's banker and its docks the busiest port.

sources.cite: David Kynaston, The City of London, vol. 1-2 (1994-95)
Youssef Cassis, Capitals of Capital: A History of International Financial Centres, 1780-2005 (Cambridge UP, 2006)

legs.lost: The First World War turned Britain into a debtor and moved the money centre to New York.

legs.why: Wall Street financed the Allies in 1914 to 1918 and the dollar replaced sterling; the container was invented for its harbour in 1956.

sources.cite: Youssef Cassis, Capitals of Capital: A History of International Financial Centres, 1780-2005 (Cambridge UP, 2006)
Giovanni Arrighi, The Long Twentieth Century (Verso, 1994)
Marc Levinson, The Box (Princeton UP, 2006)

view: A model-curated chain in the Braudel and Arrighi tradition; the order is a judgement

sources.cite: Fernand Braudel, Civilization and Capitalism, 15th-18th Century, vol. 3: The Perspective of the World (1979)
Giovanni Arrighi, The Long Twentieth Century (Verso, 1994)
Janet Abu-Lughod, Before European Hegemony: The World System A.D. 1250-1350 (Oxford UP, 1989)
Philippe Beaujard, The Worlds of the Indian Ocean: A Global History (Cambridge UP, 2019)

name: Eastern trade-hub relay
what: The same baton race on the monsoon seas, from the Indus dockyard to the world's busiest container port.
why: Shows that the centre of trade keeps moving, and that wars, silt and new sea routes move it.

legs.why: Harappan port with a brick basin often read as a dockyard, trading beads and cotton toward the Gulf.

sources.cite: Gregory Possehl, The Indus Civilization: A Contemporary Perspective (2002)

legs.lost: The Indus cities declined after about 1900 BCE.

legs.why: Malabar pepper port; the Muziris papyrus records one Roman cargo worth enough to buy a large estate.

sources.cite: Lionel Casson, The Periplus Maris Erythraei (Princeton UP, 1989)
P. J. Cherian, Pattanam excavation reports, Kerala Council for Historical Research (2007-2015)

legs.lost: Its harbour silted and Roman demand faded.

legs.why: Funan's port where Indian and Chinese shipping met; Roman coins and Han mirrors have been dug up there.

sources.cite: Pierre-Yves Manguin, "The Archaeology of Early Maritime Polities of Southeast Asia", in Southeast Asia from Prehistory to History (2004)

legs.lost: Ships began sailing straight through the Malacca Strait instead of crossing the isthmus.

legs.why: Capital of Srivijaya, which controlled the Malacca and Sunda straits between India and China.

sources.cite: O. W. Wolters, Early Indonesian Commerce (Cornell UP, 1967)
Lynda Shaffer, Maritime Southeast Asia to 1500 (1996)

legs.lost: Raided by the Chola navy in 1025.

legs.why: Tang China's main foreign port, home to large Arab and Persian merchant communities.

sources.cite: Hugh Clark, Community, Trade, and Networks: Southern Fujian from the 3rd to the 13th Century (Cambridge UP, 1991)

legs.lost: Huang Chao's rebels massacred its foreign merchants in 878 or 879.

legs.why: Zaitun of Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta, the great port of Song and Yuan China, with a maritime trade office from 1087.

sources.cite: Hugh Clark, Community, Trade, and Networks: Southern Fujian from the 3rd to the 13th Century (Cambridge UP, 1991)
Janet Abu-Lughod, Before European Hegemony: The World System A.D. 1250-1350 (Oxford UP, 1989)

legs.lost: Ming bans on private sea trade (from 1371) and the silting of its river.

legs.why: Malabar pepper hub open to all traders under the Zamorin; Zheng He and Vasco da Gama both landed here.

sources.cite: K. N. Chaudhuri, Trade and Civilisation in the Indian Ocean (Cambridge UP, 1985)
Michael Pearson, The Indian Ocean (Routledge, 2003)

legs.lost: Portuguese bombardment and blockade from 1500.

legs.why: The sultanate at the strait, where Tome Pires said whoever was lord of Malacca had his hand on Venice's throat.

sources.cite: Anthony Reid, Southeast Asia in the Age of Commerce, 1450-1680 (Yale UP, 1988-93)

legs.lost: Taken by the Portuguese in 1511, and its traders scattered.

legs.why: Where Mexican and Peruvian silver met Chinese silk and porcelain on the galleons, joining the world economy into one.

sources.cite: Dennis Flynn and Arturo Giraldez, "Born with a Silver Spoon: The Origin of World Trade in 1571", Journal of World History 6(2), 1995
William Lytle Schurz, The Manila Galleon (1939)

legs.lost: The last galleon sailed in 1815.

legs.why: Under the Canton System the only Chinese port open to Western ships; tea for silver, then for opium.

sources.cite: Paul Van Dyke, The Canton Trade: Life and Enterprise on the China Coast, 1700-1845 (2005)

legs.lost: The Treaty of Nanking (1842) opened other ports and ceded Hong Kong.

legs.why: Raffles' free port at the Malacca Strait, now one of the busiest transshipment ports in the world.

sources.cite: C. M. Turnbull, A History of Modern Singapore, 1819-2005 (NUS Press, 2009)

legs.why: Treaty port on the Yangtze mouth that became Asia's biggest financial centre by the 1930s.

sources.cite: Marie-Claire Bergere, Shanghai: China's Gateway to Modernity (Stanford UP, 2009)

legs.lost: Foreign firms left after the 1949 revolution.

legs.why: Took Shanghai's capital and refugees after 1949 and became the gateway to China during the closed decades.

sources.cite: Marie-Claire Bergere, Shanghai: China's Gateway to Modernity (Stanford UP, 2009)

legs.lost: Mainland ports took the cargo once China reopened.

legs.why: Busiest container port in the world every year since 2010.

sources.cite: Marc Levinson, The Box (Princeton UP, 2006)

view: A model-curated chain in the Braudel and Arrighi tradition; the order is a judgement

sources.cite: Fernand Braudel, Civilization and Capitalism, 15th-18th Century, vol. 3: The Perspective of the World (1979)
Giovanni Arrighi, The Long Twentieth Century (Verso, 1994)
Janet Abu-Lughod, Before European Hegemony: The World System A.D. 1250-1350 (Oxford UP, 1989)
Philippe Beaujard, The Worlds of the Indian Ocean: A Global History (Cambridge UP, 2019)

name: Silk Roads
why: Overland chains of caravan cities between China and the Mediterranean; few merchants went the whole way.

sources.cite: Valerie Hansen, The Silk Road: A New History (Oxford UP, 2012)
Peter Frankopan, The Silk Roads: A New History of the World (2015)

name: Persian Royal Road
why: Herodotus says royal couriers covered its 2,500 km in about a week.

sources.cite: Herodotus, Histories 5.52-54 (the Royal Road)
Pierre Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander: A History of the Persian Empire (2002)

name: Incense Route
why: Camel caravans carried South Arabian incense north to the Mediterranean; Petra grew rich taxing it.

sources.cite: Barry Cunliffe, By Steppe, Desert, and Ocean (Oxford UP, 2015)

name: Amber Road
why: Baltic amber went south to Roman workshops at Aquileia.

sources.cite: Barry Cunliffe, By Steppe, Desert, and Ocean (Oxford UP, 2015)

name: Indian Ocean monsoon route
why: Ships rode the summer monsoon east and the winter monsoon home, so the timing of trade followed the winds.

sources.cite: Lionel Casson, The Periplus Maris Erythraei (Princeton UP, 1989)
K. N. Chaudhuri, Trade and Civilisation in the Indian Ocean (Cambridge UP, 1985)
Philippe Beaujard, The Worlds of the Indian Ocean: A Global History (Cambridge UP, 2019)

name: Swahili coast and Gulf route
why: Zimbabwe gold shipped from Kilwa paid for Persian and Chinese goods.

sources.cite: Michael Pearson, The Indian Ocean (Routledge, 2003)
Philippe Beaujard, The Worlds of the Indian Ocean: A Global History (Cambridge UP, 2019)

name: Trans-Saharan gold and salt route
why: Camel caravans swapped Saharan salt and North African goods for West African gold.

sources.cite: Ralph Austen, Trans-Saharan Africa in World History (Oxford UP, 2010)

name: Route from the Varangians to the Greeks
why: Norse traders rowed down the Russian rivers to Constantinople.

sources.cite: Simon Franklin and Jonathan Shepard, The Emergence of Rus, 750-1200 (1996)

name: Hanseatic League routes
why: A league of German merchant towns ran the North Sea and Baltic trade.

sources.cite: Philippe Dollinger, The German Hansa (1970)

name: Tea Horse Road
why: Porters and mule trains carried Sichuan tea to Tibet in exchange for horses.

sources.cite: Andrew Forbes and David Henley, China's Ancient Tea Horse Road (2011)

name: Cape Route (Carreira da India)
why: Da Gama's route round Africa took spices off the Venice monopoly until the Suez Canal opened.

sources.cite: C. R. Boxer, The Portuguese Seaborne Empire, 1415-1825 (1969)
Jonathan Israel, Dutch Primacy in World Trade, 1585-1740 (Oxford UP, 1989)

name: Manila galleon
why: Spanish silver from Potosi and Mexico crossed the Pacific to buy Chinese goods.

sources.cite: Dennis Flynn and Arturo Giraldez, "Born with a Silver Spoon: The Origin of World Trade in 1571", Journal of World History 6(2), 1995
William Lytle Schurz, The Manila Galleon (1939)

name: Atlantic triangular trade
why: British goods to West Africa, enslaved Africans to the Caribbean, sugar and cotton back to Britain.

sources.cite: Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database, SlaveVoyages (estimates page)

name: Out of Africa
why: Every population outside Africa descends mainly from a small group that left roughly 50,000 to 70,000 years ago.

sources.cite: David Reich, Who We Are and How We Got Here (2018)
Chris Clarkson et al., "Human occupation of northern Australia by 65,000 years ago", Nature 547, 2017

name: Spread into Europe and East Asia
why: Modern humans reached Europe by about 45,000 years ago and met Neanderthals there.

sources.cite: David Reich, Who We Are and How We Got Here (2018)

name: Peopling of the Americas
why: People crossed from Siberia through Beringia and reached southern Chile (Monte Verde) by about 14,500 years ago.

sources.cite: Ted Goebel, Michael Waters and Dennis O'Rourke, "The Late Pleistocene Dispersal of Modern Humans in the Americas", Science 319, 2008

name: Austronesian expansion
why: Seafarers from Taiwan spread over half the globe, from Madagascar to Easter Island.

sources.cite: Peter Bellwood, First Migrants: Ancient Migration in Global Perspective (2013)
Jared Diamond and Peter Bellwood, "Farmers and Their Languages: The First Expansions", Science 300, 2003

name: Polynesian voyaging
why: Lapita voyagers reached Samoa by about 800 BCE; East Polynesia, Hawaii and New Zealand were settled quickly between about 1000 and 1300 CE.

sources.cite: Patrick Kirch, On the Road of the Winds (Univ. of California Press, 2017 ed.)
Janet Wilmshurst et al., "High-precision radiocarbon dating shows recent and rapid initial human colonization of East Polynesia", PNAS 108(5), 2011

name: Bantu expansion
why: Farmers from the Nigeria-Cameroon borderlands spread Bantu languages over most of sub-Saharan Africa.

sources.cite: Rebecca Grollemund et al., "Bantu expansion shows that habitat alters the route and pace of human dispersals", PNAS 112(43), 2015
Jared Diamond and Peter Bellwood, "Farmers and Their Languages: The First Expansions", Science 300, 2003

name: Steppe migration into Europe
why: Ancient DNA shows steppe herders replacing much of Europe's ancestry within a few centuries; most scholars link them to Indo-European languages.

sources.cite: David Reich, Who We Are and How We Got Here (2018)
David Anthony, The Horse, the Wheel, and Language (Princeton UP, 2007)

name: Indo-Aryan migration
why: Steppe ancestry arrived in South Asia in the second millennium BCE, the likely route of Sanskrit's ancestor.

sources.cite: David Reich, Who We Are and How We Got Here (2018)
David Anthony, The Horse, the Wheel, and Language (Princeton UP, 2007)

name: Germanic migrations
why: From the Gothic crossing of the Danube in 376 to the Lombard invasion of Italy in 568, these movements remade the western Roman world.

sources.cite: Guy Halsall, Barbarian Migrations and the Roman West, 376-568 (Cambridge UP, 2007)

name: Slavic expansion
why: Slavic speakers spread from eastern Europe to the Baltic, the Elbe and the Balkans in about two centuries.

sources.cite: Paul Barford, The Early Slavs (2001)

name: Magyar settlement
why: Steppe horsemen settled the Carpathian Basin, founding Hungary.

sources.cite: Peter Golden, Central Asia in World History (Oxford UP, 2011)

name: Norse expansion
why: Raiders and settlers from Scandinavia reached Iceland (874), Greenland (985) and Newfoundland (about 1000).

sources.cite: Stefan Brink and Neil Price (eds), The Viking World (Routledge, 2008)

name: Turkic migration into Anatolia
why: After Manzikert (1071) Turkmen herders moved into Anatolia, turning Byzantine land into Turkey.

sources.cite: A. C. S. Peacock, The Great Seljuk Empire (Edinburgh UP, 2015)

name: Mongol expansion
why: The largest contiguous land empire moved armies, artisans and whole peoples across Eurasia.

sources.cite: Peter Golden, Central Asia in World History (Oxford UP, 2011)

name: Transatlantic slave trade
why: About 12.5 million people were forced onto ships and about 10.7 million survived the crossing; the largest forced migration in history.

sources.cite: Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database, SlaveVoyages (estimates page)

name: Irish famine emigration
why: The potato famine killed about a million people and drove one to two million to emigrate within a decade.

sources.cite: Christine Kinealy, This Great Calamity: The Irish Famine 1845-52 (1994)

name: European mass migration
why: Steamships and cheap land drew tens of millions of Europeans to the Americas and Australasia.

sources.cite: Adam McKeown, "Global Migration, 1846-1940", Journal of World History 15(2), 2004, pp. 155-189
Timothy Hatton and Jeffrey Williamson, The Age of Mass Migration (Oxford UP, 1998)

name: Indian and southern Chinese migration
why: A second mass migration, of similar size to the Atlantic one, went from India and southern China to Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean rim.

sources.cite: Adam McKeown, "Global Migration, 1846-1940", Journal of World History 15(2), 2004, pp. 155-189

name: Migration to Manchuria and Siberia
why: The third great migration of the era, mostly northern Chinese moving to Manchuria, often overlooked.

sources.cite: Adam McKeown, "Global Migration, 1846-1940", Journal of World History 15(2), 2004, pp. 155-189

name: Great Migration (United States)
why: About six million Black Southerners moved to northern and western cities, escaping Jim Crow.

sources.cite: Isabel Wilkerson, The Warmth of Other Suns (2010)
James Gregory, The Southern Diaspora (UNC Press, 2005)

name: Partition of India
why: Census data suggest about 14.5 million people crossed the new borders and millions more went missing.

sources.cite: Prashant Bharadwaj, Asim Khwaja and Atif Mian, "The Big March: Migratory Flows after the Partition of India", Economic and Political Weekly 43(35), 2008
